bug_semantics: picklescan disassembles pickle GLOBAL/STACK_GLOBAL references and, in the default scan result, counts a finding only when the referenced module/name matches its hard-coded unsafe-globals blocklist. Through v0.0.34 the blocklist omitted both the serialized global _io.FileIO and urllib.request.urlopen, so a crafted pickle could open an arbitrary local file and pass that file object as the body of an attacker-directed HTTP request without either global being counted as dangerous. A consumer relying on the scan could then deserialize the payload, causing arbitrary file read plus SSRF/data exfiltration.
flaw_origin: The initial scanner implementation introduced the incomplete-denylist security model: src/picklescan/scanner.py enumerated selected suspicious globals and scan_pickle_bytes incremented issues_count only for exact blocklist matches, silently leaving unlisted callable globals such as _io.FileIO and urllib.request.urlopen outside the failing result. Later classification of unknown globals as Suspicious did not cure the default-pass behavior because only Dangerous globals incremented issues_count; the vulnerable mechanism therefore originates in the initial scanner commit rather than in a later refactor or blocklist expansion.
ai_marker: absent: the BIC commit object names author Matthieu Maitre <mmaitre314@users.noreply.github.com> and committer Matthieu Maitre <mmaitre314@users.noreply.github.com>; its complete message is 'Implement Pickle scanner' with no Co-Authored-By, Generated-with, or other trailers, and neither identity is a bot.
evidence: First-party advisory https://github.com/mmaitre314/picklescan/security/advisories/GHSA-9726-w42j-3qjr specifies affected versions <0.0.35, patched version 0.0.35, and the io.FileIO -> urllib.request.urlopen exfiltration chain. PR https://github.com/mmaitre314/picklescan/pull/55 and release https://github.com/mmaitre314/picklescan/releases/tag/v0.0.35 identify the remediation. In the validated clone, `git log -L 14,24:src/picklescan/scanner.py c1d5abd...` attributes the original suspicious-globals dictionary to c1d5abdcc740e0d08a0d12d015d08e1e6f29a67e, and `git log -L 77,89:src/picklescan/scanner.py c1d5abd...` shows that same new-file commit introduced scan_pickle_bytes with exact blocklist lookup and issues_count increment only on a match. `git cat-file -e 6a76b8c3ac67dc04181e600614ecf2a423cca326:src/picklescan/scanner.py` fails because the path is absent, while `git ls-tree -r --name-only` for that parent shows no src tree, directly verifying parent absence. The BIC's setup.cfg reports version 0.0.1; `git describe --contains --tags` reports c1d5abd... is contained by v0.0.2~12, and `git merge-base c1d5abd... v0.0.34` returns c1d5abd..., proving the mechanism precedes the last vulnerable tag. At v0.0.34, src/picklescan/scanner.py:356-391 maps non-blocklisted globals to Suspicious but increments issues_count only for Dangerous entries, and its unsafe table at lines 110-186 contains neither _io.FileIO nor urllib.request. `git log -S` for both `"_io": {"FileIO"}` and `"urllib.request": "*"` finds only a01c58d5dd7960db557b849817c0ab83ab111ef1. That commit adds both unsafe entries plus regression pickles/tests and changes setup.cfg 0.0.34 -> 0.0.35; v0.0.34 resolves to its immediate parent 323bd004691e442b109b00a1251cd9acc1a4be98, v0.0.35 resolves exactly to a01c58d5dd7960db557b849817c0ab83ab111ef1, and `git describe --contains --tags a01c58d...` returns v0.0.35. Finally, `git cat-file -p c1d5abd...` supplies the human author/committer and trailer-free message quoted in ai_marker.
reasoning: The vulnerability is a scanner-detection bypass, not execution performed by picklescan itself: the scanner exposes pickle globals, but its default failing result is driven by a finite dangerous-global dictionary. The advisory's payload serializes io.FileIO as _io.FileIO to open a local file and then invokes urllib.request.urlopen with that file as an iterable request body, so omitting both globals permits the malicious pickle to avoid a Dangerous finding and creates the unsafe trust decision before downstream unpickling. History tracing distinguishes the true origin from later churn: f98f9bd89b16ab1b1b1b6366acddd1b2a4d36fe9 merely renamed _suspicious_globals to _unsafe_globals during PyTorch work, whereas c1d5abdcc740e0d08a0d12d015d08e1e6f29a67e created both the finite blocklist and exact-match reporting logic in one direct, single-parent implementation commit. Its immediate parent has no scanner source at all, so the vulnerable mechanism is directly absent there; no squash/member decomposition or move is needed. The BIC shipped in the initial 0.0.1 code and is ancestral to v0.0.34, while the direct fix a01c58d5dd7960db557b849817c0ab83ab111ef1 is exactly tag v0.0.35 and adds the two missing dangerous globals. AI attribution is restricted to the BIC commit object: it has human author and committer identities, a plain one-line message, and no AI/co-author/generated trailers. Therefore the proven smallest BIC is human-authored and the closed verdict is NOT_AI.
